title: Around the Bend
full_review:
You might think a story about two men and a child traveling around the Southwest to scatter the ashes of the family patriarch would be a total turnoff. Yet, in spite of this seemingly downbeat theme, "Around the Bend" (Warner Independent) is an affecting, albeit offbeat, tale of the loving bond among four generations of males, and a touching story of healing and forgiveness.

Eccentric family patriarch Henry Lair (Michael Caine) lives with his recently separated grandson, Jason (Josh Lucas), who works in a bank, and 6-year-old great-grandson, Zack (Jonah Bobo), as well as a daffy Danish nanny (Glenne Headly) who is unaccountably enamored of horror films.

One day, a scruffy man shows up on their doorstep, and it turns out to be Jason's father, Turner (Christopher Walken), an ex-heroin addict who abandoned the family when Jason was 2. Henry is overjoyed that his long-lost son has returned at last, and insists the four go out and celebrate at his idea of the paragon of elegant dining: Kentucky Fried Chicken.

Turner's plan to leave town after this emotionally tumultuous homecoming is thwarted by Henry's death in the KFC restaurant, after which Turner and Jason discover Henry had left detailed instructions on how he'd like his remains handled. Having predicted his beloved dog would die shortly after he did, Henry asks that their ashes be commingled and scattered in an elaborate ritual that involves traveling through the desert to Albuquerque, N.M., and eating at specific KFCs until they reach the final destination.

Along the way, Jason finally vents his long-pent-up frustration at his early abandonment by Turner, while the latter comes to value the son -- and now grandson -- he had never known. Zack observes the dynamic between the adults with a wisdom well beyond his years.

The film climaxes with the highly charged revelation of circumstances of why Turner walked out on the family years before, but ends on a sweet and poignant note.

On the whole, this is a lovely, small-scale film that holds your interest throughout its 85 minutes. The performances are predictably fine, and even though Caine's character dies very near the beginning, his presence lingers memorably throughout. Young Bobo is particularly endearing, and gives one of those astonishingly good kid performances.

Jordan Roberts -- who was inspired by his own relationship with an absentee father to explore themes of grief and estrangement -- has written a script that doesn't always avoid cliche, and though for the most part the film successfully avoids cheap sentiment, there are some occasional lapses.

Some cheerfully eclectic songs on the soundtrack are astutely used to undercut the downbeat aspects of the story, though Leon Russell's "A Song for You" is oddly jarring when it comes up during a pivotal plot development.

There is some salty language, some of which is said in the presence of Zack -- and the spreading of the ashes would be considered disrespectful from a Catholic viewpoint -- but the themes of forgiveness and reconciliation are what really matter here.

Because of some rough and crude language, brief bloody images and an irreligious dispersal of ashes, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
